newsitem.title: INDIA: India strives to plug corporate tax loopholes.
newsitem.headline: India strives to plug corporate tax loopholes.

text.p: India is likely to reconfigure a minimum alternate tax (MAT) in its federal budget due later this week, but the controversial levy will be reworked at a price, analysts said on Wednesday.
MAT -- a 12.9 percent minimum tax on profits -- was imposed by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in the 1996/97 budget last July to bring some of India's top firms into the tax dragnet.

MAT was a blow to companies already reeling under the impact of a slowdown in the Indian economy. Bombay's benchmark stocks index fell sharply after the budget to hit a three-year low of 2713.12 points in December.

But share prices have rebounded nine percent in the new year on hopes of a market-friendly 1997/98 budget -- due to be unveiled on February 28. Some analysts said there was a chance MAT could be repealed to placate industry and markets.

"Since there's so much pressure and everything is being blamed on MAT (minimum alternate tax), I think to this extent it may be repealed," said Dinesh Vyas, a top corporate tax lawyer and a director on the boards of several companies.
But he said Chidambaram would probably have in place measures which would raise taxable profits of all companies to increase revenues.

Vyas, who is a member of the federal government's Central Direct Taxes Advisory Committee, headed by the finance minister, believes Chidambaram will cut the ceiling on depreciation allowed under the Income-Tax (I-T) Act.
"What will happen is the (depreciation) rate in income tax will be reduced and brought in parity with the Companies Act," he told Reuters. "This will indirectly affect all companies."
Permissible depreciation ranges from 5.0 percent on assets that have a longer life to 100 percent on pollution control equipment or energy saving devices.

Currently, the tax law provides for higher write-offs for depreciation as compared to the Companies Act. As the tax is levied on the net profit -- after setting off depreciation -- this helps companies to reduce the taxable profit.
Some firms show higher profits under the Companies Act and pay regular dividends, but report lower profits for tax purposes because of higher depreciation allowances.

Other companies record profits year after year but pay no taxes thanks to generous exemptions. "The whole reasoning for MAT was that companies were regularly paying dividends, but not taxes," said Nihal Kothari, head of taxation at Hindustan Lever Ltd, the subsidiary of Anglo-Dutch conglomerate Unilever Plc.
Many blue-chip companies like petrochemicals giant Reliance Industries Ltd and Tata Iron and Steel Company Ltd enjoyed zero-tax status by ploughing back profits into tax-spared new ventures.
The Income Tax Act gave tax reliefs, incentives, benefits, exemptions and reductions to industry with the objective of luring businesses into rural areas and generate jobs.
Analysts said MAT sought to undo these basic tenets.
"MAT was a contradiction to the spirit of law," said Vyas. "It was an unwanted guest."
He said companies set up plants in remote interiors of the country because they were promised the incentives. MAT changed the rules in mid-stream.
Hindustan Lever's Kothari said Chidambaram could follow the British model where companies are levied a tax on dividend payouts, which can be set off against shareholders' tax liability.
This enables the government to generate revenue irrespective of taxable profits. It also does away with double taxation of dividends -- a long standing demand.
India taxes shareholders on their dividend income although the dividend is paid out of taxed profits.
ICICI Securities and Finance Company Ltd (I-Sec) analyst M.R. Madhavan said MAT had harmed the economics of projects underway, which were based on feasibility studies made before MAT was introduced.
"MAT is unlikely to be revoked although there is a distinct possibility of it changing hues under the Income Tax Act or the Companies Act," I-Sec said in a report.
